text: Major antibiotic families used in animals: Beta-lactamines (Penicillin, Ampicillin, Amoxicillin, Cephalosporins), Polypeptides (Colistin), Quinolones (Flumequine, Enrofloxacin), Aminosides (Gentamycin, Streptomycin), Sulfamides (Sulfadimidine, Sulfamethoxine, Trimethoprim/TMP), Phenicols (Florfenicol, Thiamphenicol, Chloramphenicol — banned in many countries), Tetracyclines (Oxytetracycline, Doxycycline), and Macrolides (Tylosin, Spiramycin, Erythromycin, with Lincomycin and Tiamulin closely related). Combining two antibiotics can widen the effective spectrum, e.g. Ampicillin (kills Gram+) with Colistin (kills Gram-) gives broader coverage than either alone; other known combinations are Penicillin+Streptomycin (Penstrep) and Sulfonamide+TMP (Septotryl). Never combine more than 2 antibiotics — the effect of mixing 3+ is unpredictable, and a product combining that many is a sign it is not from a reliable manufacturer. Synergism (combination works better than either alone) is seen with Ampicillin+Colistin, Sulfonamide+TMP, and Tetracycline+Macrolide/Sulfonamide combinations. Antagonism (combination works worse than either alone) occurs with Betalactamine+Macrolide or Betalactamine+Tetracycline — products combining amoxicillin and oxytetracycline, or containing Chloramphenicol, are signs of an unreliable manufacturer and should not be bought.
